work.author: Severian of Gabala
work.title: Oratio in dedicationem pretiosae et uiuificae crucis

paragraphs.text: Again there is a feast for the church, and again a mystery: the joy of the faithful, the salvation of souls, a sweet fragrance for the world. Today we celebrate the festival of the Dedication of the life-bearing Cross. The heavens rejoice, the angels join the dance, and God is glorified. Long ago, when it was planted at the Place of the Skull, it made victory over death blossom. Now it has appeared to the whole world and revealed the trophy won over the devil. That day was glorious, and this day too shines its bright rays upon us, for it also shares in that mystery and draws the whole of its wonder from it, even though the mystery of the cross is not new. On that day the cross proclaimed the Master's victory and power. The wood did not work those wonders beyond reason; the One upon it worked marvels possible to God alone. This day, because of the mystery accomplished then, shows us the power of the cross itself. The truth of what happened bears witness to this account. It was not the sight of wood that made the sun hide itself in fear, nor was it a voice from wood that shook the earth. The sun trembled, and the earth shuddered with it, when it saw the Master willingly enduring in his own flesh the outrages the wicked heaped on him. But now the cross, which evildoers devised to outrage and dishonor the Creator, is displayed in glory and works wonders beyond belief. Angels see it and revere it because of the mystery wrought on it. Demons behold it and are put to flight. Angels see it and escort it like a guard of honor, acclaiming the peace that came through it from the One nailed to it. Demons contemplate it and are driven off, scourged by blows they cannot see.

But why have we let the momentum of the sermon carry us on to the last things and left the first behind? The occasion requires us to recall why today we seem, as some suppose, to give a kind of beginning to the cross, which, as I said, the Jews devised long ago to outrage the Master. We are not giving a beginning, lovers of the feast, to what already exists. We are delighting in the one who reigns and presides. David did not begin to reign when the people inaugurated his kingdom anew. He called the submission of the whole race of Israel a public feast and a dedication. In the same way, we do not give a fresh beginning to what was shining long before. Together with every nation and race, with tribes and tongues and peoples, we keep a feast that is above the world and spans the whole world, celebrating the agreement of all in submission to the saving cross of our Lord. This is not our invention. It had already been foreordained in God's foreknowledge, even if the God-hating and Lord-slaying Jews built it when the time came. We keep the feast because the cross was then planted in the middle of the earth like the sun in a dark and freezing winter. Through the Sun of righteousness upon it, it suddenly sent its rays over the earth. It melted the frost of the devil's tyranny and drove off the winter of impiety. Like the air, it brought the human and rational mind into a mild balance, and it quickened the neglected souls of men so that they sprouted the cultivation of every good work and all virtue. Then it was hidden by the dark malice of the Jews, as when a cloud runs beneath the sun. Now the unsetting light of the tree of life has risen brightly upon the earth again. For this reason we call the day a Dedication, and we keep an all-praised feast of what has already been celebrated and glorified.

The Jews, as always, were cheated of the truth this time too. Out of envy they buried the divine treasure under the earth, so that not everyone would be enriched. But it did not stay hidden, nor did it overlook for long the loss suffered by the poor. Like the sun, it broke through the cloud of malice that held it and was spread over it, and burned that cloud away by the heat of its own light and might. It spread its radiance over the whole creation, brightened the world, warmed all the naked, and enriched the earth. The listener may wonder, I think, why the raving Jews did not destroy this saving wood completely, by fire or by some other means, and instead hid it. We will answer him that hiding it was also meant to destroy it. But the power concealed within it is divine. By God's plan, and for many necessary purposes as it seems to me, it allowed them to carry out what they intended, so that it might be glorified all the more by this as well. Yet it walled their malice off from its final aim, the destruction of the cross, which was their plan and the plan of the disobedient who came after them. So they forced themselves to bury the ever-flowing spring and hurried to foul the channel of the life-bearing streams. But the fools labored in vain, for it is written: "Evil will not prevail over wisdom." They senselessly tried to force back the current of the river that gladdens the city of God, and so its uncontrollable deep laughed at them. Like a tide, it rotted away the barriers they had set on it and flooded the inhabited world, as it is written: "Like a river overflowing with peace, and like a torrent flooding with the glory of the nations." It was necessary, then, truly necessary, that the divine wisdom which surpasses all understanding should let them do what they desired. They had acted shamelessly against the saving passion. Through the signs that took place, all creation had spat on them. Even so they did not repent, but, as Isaiah says, "they were put to shame and did not recognize their dishonor." So they were to leave to later generations, as pledges of their rashness and recklessness, the proof of their unbelief concerning the life-giving cross. And the faithful were to receive with greater longing the inexhaustible treasure of life by which they were sealed for eternal life. Things that come to us of their own accord are not loved as much as things found with longing and effort. The wretches knew what the prophets had said about the cross. One said: "Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me." The rod is the shepherd's rod against the wolves, and the staff is a support that sets upright those who have fallen and been broken by the serpent. Another said: "Blessed is the wood through which righteousness comes." Another: "Those who are sealed so as not to learn the law will be made manifest." And another: "You have given to those who fear you a sign, so that they may flee from the face of the bow." So, driven by the envy of wickedness, they were eager to darken what was good. Once the foolish people had said in its heart, "Christ is not God," they left no stone unturned in their unbelief to confirm their own unbelief. That is why they revile him even when he is dead, guard the tomb, bury the cross, and "grow strong in their vanity." But their efforts turned out the opposite way. The hopes of wicked men are unstable: they imagine what they desire and what suits their own villainy, and then they suffer the reverse. At the tomb they kept watch in vain to prevent the resurrection. In the same way here, they laid the tree of life in the bosom of the earth like a cutting, and so they sanctified the earth and made the tree more beautiful and more fruitful in the fruits of immortality. And the marvel is that it was kept incorrupt in the earth for some three hundred and thirty years, a treasure that is never spent. What farmers, in love with their own loss! They planted, and left the fruit to us. They had the treasure, chose to be poor, and made us rich. That is why I dance and celebrate this worldwide feast. A plant of life has sprung up and been raised high toward heaven. A ladder to heaven has appeared for the faithful. God has built an unbreakable wall for those whose land was ravaged. A harbor has appeared for the storm-tossed. A beacon has been kindled for those in darkness. An invincible weapon has been forged for the weak. A refuge has been found for the persecuted. So it is fitting to say today as well: "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men." Today the trees of paradise exult and clap their branches. A remedy has been found for the tree of disobedience. Now Adam rightly gathers the fruit of the tree of life and will live forever. Man, who was cast out of paradise, delights once more in the good things of paradise. I keep this feast that is above the world because "the Lord has raised up a horn of salvation for his people." The cross, even when it is only traced in the air, has as much power as faith can hold. Demons dread it and are put to flight when they behold the mystery in it. It is the support of the world, the salvation of souls, the weapon of those who fight bravely. It sanctifies the height and the depth and the ends of the inhabited world on either side. Jacob saw it as a ladder, "and the angels ascending and descending on it." Through it enmity was abolished and peace was awarded to those in heaven and on earth. Angels come down to anoint the athletes, and the workers of godliness go up to receive the prizes of the upward call from God, who presides over the contest. That is why it says: "And the Lord stood firmly upon it." Moses prefigured the cross and routed Amalek. He saw the enemy fighting the people down, crushing them, and ravaging the camp with weapons. He found no human help against the evil and no way to stop the disasters. So he lifted his mind to God and set his feet toward the summit of the crag. By stretching out his hands he raised the invincible symbol of the cross against the enemy and drove them back by it. Through that victory he foretold the celebrated victory of the Savior, I mean the victory on the cross. But "the enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction," contradict this account. They claim that the stretching out of the prophet's hands was a figure of prayer and not of the cross. But Scripture did not credit the victory to prayer. It credited it to the figure and posture of the hands. It says: "Moses went up the mountain and spread out his hands. Whenever Moses stretched out his hands, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hands, Amalek prevailed." If it had been the work of prayer, it should have said, as it did in Egypt, "Moses stretched out his hands to God, and Israel prevailed." But it does not say that. It left prayer out, not because prayer is useless, but because prayer had to step aside so that this victory could be credited to the figure of the cross. In Egypt, it says, Moses cried out to God and the wrath abated. Here it does not say so. If you force the text, you make the prophet's prayer unacceptable to God. Raising and lowering the hands many times is the sign of someone who is not heard, not of someone who is heard. "But Moses grew tired," he says, "overcome by the weight." Very true. But the type of the voluntary and celebrated passion did not grow tired. For this very reason Aaron and Hur stand and hold up his hands, so that the victory would not be undone when the figure was undone. So priesthood and kingship escort the figure of the cross like a guard of honor, since Aaron holds the rank of the priesthood and Hur bore the dignity of the royal court.

Do you see, Jew, how brightly the truth shines through the types? Have you ever seen someone praying to God while others held him up, and sitting down at that? But on this point the sermon has said enough for those whose ears do not itch and who do not turn away from the word of truth. Again, the type of the cross sweetened the water of Marah, for it is written: "The Lord showed Moses a piece of wood, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet." It also drove the serpents away from the people. Scripture says that because of their grumbling, God sent deadly serpents among them. Why, then, does that great and most wise Moses not oppose the divine command? Why does he not fight God's order by force and hold back the wrath again with his hands in the shape of a cross? Against Amalek he raised the divine weapon against something God had not set in motion. Here, since the sentence came from God, he appeals to God's love for mankind and calms the threat with supplications. Against the wrath of the One who strikes, he applies the command itself as a healing remedy, like a soothing poultice. For God says: "Make a bronze serpent and set it on a pole. If a serpent bites a man, everyone who has been bitten will look at it and live." What does this pattern mean? What does the shadow announce? How did the image of the accursed bring life to your ancestors?

"O foolish and disobedient in heart," how long will you contradict the truth? You who love the darkness and hate the light, why do you stumble at the cross of Christ? I hold to what is yours. I accept your histories, and I accept that a dead bronze serpent teemed with life for dying men. I believe this and do not depart from the text. You, though, do not even keep in step with the typological history of Scripture, and you contradict the truth in which it was fulfilled. Why do you treat devotion to Christ as impiety and say, "It is written: Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree"? Have you not heard what was said of the serpent: "Cursed are you above all the beasts"? How, then, did the image of the accursed bring salvation to a people storm-tossed by disaster? Would it not have been more believable to say: "If any of you is bitten, let him look up to heaven, to God, and he will be saved," or "Let him look to the tabernacle of God, and he will be delivered"? Yet Moses passed over all of these and set up only the figure of the cross, and did so by means of the accursed serpent. Why did Moses do this, when he had told the people: "You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or a cast image, or any likeness of anything in heaven above, or on the earth below, or in the waters under the earth"? But why do I say these things to an unreasonable man? I will ask the lawgiver himself. Tell me, most faithful servant of God: do you do what you forbid? Do you build what you tear down? You said, "You shall not make a carved image," and you ground the molten calf to powder. Are you now casting a serpent in bronze? And not in secret, but openly, for all to know? "I made those laws," he says, "to cut away the material of impiety and lead the people away from all apostasy and idolatry. But now I cast the serpent for a useful purpose, as a prefiguration of the truth. I pitched the tabernacle and everything in it, and I spread out the cherubim, a likeness of the invisible beings, over the holy place as a type and shadow of things to come. In the same way I set up the serpent as a monument for the people's salvation. Through their experience of these things they were to be trained beforehand in the figure of the sign of the cross and to learn of the Savior and Redeemer upon it." And to show that this account is entirely true, beloved, listen to the Lord confirming it: "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life." Tell me, foolish Jew, why do you stumble at the cross of Christ, which you yourself set up? Why do you hold on to that sign and keep the serpent on it? You burned incense to it until the days of King Hezekiah, and yet you resist the truth. And you do this after the conversion of the world, after the reign of godliness that has shone throughout the whole world through the cross, after the faith of the nations, the raising up and sanctifying of the churches, and God's blessing upon his people.

But the unreasonable man will say again: "If everyone who hangs on a tree is cursed, how can a blessing be given by such a one to those who believe in him?" You have heard it many times already and do not believe it: the figure of the serpent was an image of Christ's saving plan, and in this way. That figure of a serpent did not have a serpent's venom or wickedness. So too the Savior appeared "in the likeness of sinful flesh," yet was free of all sin, and he "condemned sin in the flesh," that is, the devil. As the prophet Isaiah says: "He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth." That bronze serpent had the image and form of a serpent but had no venom and no wickedness. While the others shot out their venom, it bit no one and struck no one, and yet it was itself crucified in place of the ones that bit. In the same way, while other men sinned, the sinless Jesus suffers for all. Among other things, Isaiah rightly foretold this when he said: "Because of the sins of the people he was led to death, and the Lord handed him over for our sins." Chew over the word again. There, some were bitten because of their sins and were dying, and another was crucified for them, in order to save us and destroy those who were ruining our race. There, two things happened together: the killers were abolished and the dying were made alive. So here too the death of Christ became the death of death, and made the life of incorruption well up for the dying. If Christ had not descended into Hades, if Life had not entered into death through a mortal body, those in death would not have returned to life. Through disobedience corruption had become attached to our nature, so whoever wished to save us had to abolish that corrupting substance itself. This could happen in no other way than by joining Life, which is life by nature, to the one who had received corruption. Life would abolish the corruption, and through its close struggle with death it would remake him, with all its power, as immortal from then on, by putting to death the death that held him. Elisha foreshadowed this when he worked wonders at the Jordan through extraordinary signs: by making the wood sink, he made the iron rise up.

It has now been clearly shown that the enemies of the cross have no grounds to reproach us for the form of the cross. As for you, beloved, when you hear of the cross and of the saving plan carried out in the body, lift your mind to the height of the Only-begotten's authority. Do not let the form he took for your sake lower your thinking. Let the love for mankind of the One who saved you lift you up. The cross is for your sake, but God's dignity is not pulled down by words. Those who try to pull it down bring about their own downfall, and those who exalt it raise their own lowliness to the heights.

Come, then, let us celebrate the Exaltation of the Cross together. The heavenly treasure has been opened to us, and the tree of life has been revealed to mortals. Let us cry out too: "Far be it from us to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ." What boasting do I mean? Our reconciliation to our God through it, and through it God's ineffable love and kindness toward us, because through it "we have received grace upon grace." When calamities came, the synagogue sent a censer and incense of compounded spices to God as an ambassador for the salvation of the people, reminding the One from whom nothing is hidden of the oaths and covenants made with the fathers. But the church holds up the cross of the Savior before her face to God the Father as a censer. It gives off no smoke of compounded incense. It carries the sacrifice of his Lamb and only-begotten Son as a fragrant aroma. The church does not read out again the oaths and covenants of the fathers. She holds out the sign of the love with which he loved us, the love through which he gave his only-begotten Son for us. To the Son she offers the cross as the silent herald of his ineffable condescension and of the voluntary and saving passion in his own flesh, and through it she sings: "Remember your compassion, O Lord." Remember that "while we were still sinners, you died for us." Remember your triumph over the devil on the cross. Remember the sprinkling of your holy, precious, and life-giving blood upon me through the cross. Remember how on it you tore up the handwritten bond that stood against me. Remember how on it you stretched out your spotless hands to the Father for the reconciliation of the world. Remember the glorious and most honorable outrage you suffered on it. Remember that through it, as with a hook, you baited death to take your body, and so destroyed it. Remember that on it, like an eagle, you spread your wings over us, so that dwelling under its shadow we might "not be afraid of the terror by night, nor of the arrow that flies by day, nor of the thing that walks in darkness." Remember that, mounted on it, you "trampled the asp and the basilisk, the lion and the dragon." They began to be trampled through you, who are mighty in all things, so that they might also dread the shadow of the cross traced upon us who worship you and turned against them. Remember, good shepherd, that on it you laid down your life for your flock, so that through it, as with a rod, the soul-destroying wolves might be driven away from your sheep. Plead these things for us, O cross, before the One who needs no persuading, who is ready to show compassion and quick to sympathize. For these reasons I dance. The cross has been exalted, and those who exalted themselves against us have been brought low. A royal and inviolable seal has been made public, and the plotters have fled. A wall has been built, and the enemy has cowered. The light has shone, and the darkness has been cleared away. And the church glorifies the uncreated Trinity, equal in honor and of one substance, forever venerated and forever worshiped, the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit, now and always and to the ages of ages. Amen.
